category: commentary (Hasidic homiletical commentary on the Torah and the festivals)

date.note: First printed at the turn of the nineteenth century by Levi Yitzchak of Berdichev (c. 1740-1809); the year 1798 marks the first edition, with later expanded editions gathering his homilies on the festivals. The digitized Hebrew and English text on Sefaria (including the Eliyahu Munk translation of Genesis and the Sefaria Community Translation of festival homilies) carries the passages read for this entry.

summary: Kedushat Levi ('the Holiness of Levi') is the classic Hasidic commentary on the Torah and the festivals by Levi Yitzchak of Berdichev (c. 1740-1809), a disciple of the Maggid of Mezeritch, first printed at the turn of the nineteenth century. Its recurring themes, given as the work's own attributed teaching, are joy in the service of God, the love of Israel, the doctrine of continuous creation, and the advocacy of the tzaddik, and it includes homilies for the festivals. On the open Sefaria text (Genesis, Bereshit, comment 1) it teaches that God, having created the universe, 'never withdraws from the universe for even a single moment', so that His creative activity is never completed but sustains all things at every moment.
description:
Kedushat Levi ('the Holiness of Levi') is the principal literary work of Levi Yitzchak ben Meir of Berdichev (Berdychiv, in Volhynia, c. 1740-1809), a disciple of Dov Ber, the Maggid of Mezeritch, and one of the best-known masters of the third Hasidic generation. It is a homiletical commentary on the Torah, arranged by the weekly portions and by the festivals, first printed at the turn of the nineteenth century and studied since within Hasidism as a classic of its thought. The account that follows presents the book's teaching as the work's own attributed doctrine and the tradition's, described and not affirmed or denied by the editor.

The recurring emphases of Kedushat Levi, given here as its attributed teaching, run through the commentary. First is the demand that God be served with joy and love: the service of God is presented as a matter of gladness and desire rather than of fear alone. Second is the love of Israel and the reading of the created order as existing for the sake of the covenant with Israel, the emphasis for which Levi Yitzchak is remembered in the tradition as the advocate of his people. Third is the doctrine of continuous creation: on the open Sefaria text (Genesis, Bereshit, comment 1, in the Eliyahu Munk translation) the book states as 'an axiom, general principle, that G'd created the entire universe, and having done so, never withdraws from the universe for even a single moment', so that, unlike a human craftsman who finishes a work and departs from it, the Creator's 'creative activity is never completed' but sustains all existence continually, a point the commentary ties to the present-tense language of the daily liturgy ('He creates and fashions light'). Fourth is the figure of the tzaddik, the righteous leader whose role in drawing down divine blessing and pleading the cause of Israel is a standing theme of the book and of the Hasidic teaching it represents.

Alongside the commentary on the weekly Torah portions, Kedushat Levi gathers homilies for the festivals, among them Pesach, Shavuot, Purim, and Chanukah. These festival homilies characteristically turn the observance inward and toward spiritual renewal: in the homily for Purim (Exodus, Homily for Purim, comment 1, on the open Sefaria text), the war against Amalek is read as an inward struggle, so that 'every person in Israel needs to erase the evil part that is concealed in one's heart, that is known by the name Amalek', and Israel's strength is located in the voice of Torah and prayer; and in the homilies for Chanukah (Genesis, Homilies for Chanukah, comment 1), the month of Kislev is linked to the tribe of Levi and thence to the Hasmonean priests through whom, on the reading given, the miracle came about. These readings are recorded as the homilies' own attributed interpretation of the festivals, not as the editor's.

Kedushat Levi is presented here on the tradition's own terms as Levi Yitzchak of Berdichev's Hasidic commentary on the Torah and the festivals, with its recurring themes (joy in serving God, the love of Israel, continuous divine creation, and the advocacy of the tzaddik) and its festival homilies described and attributed to the work and its author, and its theology recorded as the tradition's rather than adjudicated.

sources.citation: Green, Arthur. Defender of the Faithful: The Life and Thought of Rabbi Levi Yitshak of Berdychiv. The Tauber Institute Series for the Study of European Jewry. Waltham, MA: Brandeis University Press, 2022. The standard modern scholarly biography and theological study of Levi Yitzchak in English, treating the Kedushat Levi and its themes (the love of Israel, the advocacy of the tzaddik, continuous creation) and Levi Yitzchak's role as the 'defense attorney' (sanegoro shel Yisrael) of his people; cited as the contemporary-Jewish-scholarship lens on the work and its author. Verified to exist and be on-topic (Brandeis University Press record; described as the first scholarly biography of Levi Yitzchak in English in over thirty-five years), not read line-by-line; carries the same medium rating it holds in levi-yitzchak-of-berdichev.json.

Scholem, Gershom. Major Trends in Jewish Mysticism. New York: Schocken Books, 1941 (and later editions). The ninth lecture, 'Hasidism: The Latest Phase', is the classic academic account of the Hasidic movement and its teaching, the setting of Levi Yitzchak's Kedushat Levi and its doctrines of joy, love of Israel, and the tzaddik; cited as the academic-historian lens on the Hasidic thought the work represents. Verified to exist and be on-topic (Schocken / Princeton University Press editions), not read line-by-line; the entry does not rest on it for any specific quotation from Kedushat Levi.
